pgvector_vs_alternatives: For a personal knowledge base of 10k-50k markdown pages, pgvector is the clear winner among vector databases. It integrates directly into existing PostgreSQL, provides ACID transactions, handles real-time updates natively (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE with no index rebuilds when using HNSW), and requires zero additional infrastructure. At this scale, pgvector with HNSW index delivers sub-10ms queries with 99%+ recall. Qdrant offers better tail latency and payload filtering but adds operational complexity (separate service, no native hybrid search, smaller ecosystem) that's unjustified under 1M vectors. ChromaDB is prototyping-only—fine for demos but lacks production reliability (no proper persistence, single-node only). Milvus and Weaviate are enterprise-scale overkill—they shine at 100M+ vectors but require significant engineering resources for deployment and maintenance. FAISS (via sqlite-vec or in-memory) is viable for read-heavy workloads but requires manual serialization, has no SQL interface, and sqlite-vec's ANN support is still maturing (HNSW/IVF not yet production-ready). LanceDB is an emerging embedded option but has limited adoption. The consensus across 2025-2026 benchmarks: if you already run Postgres and have <10M vectors, pgvector is the lowest-risk, lowest-maintenance choice. It handles the 'real-time updates' requirement trivially—just upsert rows when files change. The only scenario where a dedicated vector DB wins is if you need complex filtering at scale or sub-millisecond tail latency, neither of which applies to a personal knowledge base.
embedding_models: For local/iGPU inference (~8GB VRAM), the best options balance quality, speed, and memory: (1) nomic-embed-text v1.5 (137M params, 768 dims, 8192 token context, MTEB 62.4) — the de facto standard for local RAG. At ~23MB quantized, it runs alongside any chat model without VRAM contention. Its 8192-token context is critical for markdown notes (most embedders cap at 512 tokens, silently truncating). Uses Matryoshka representation for dimension truncation. (2) qwen3-embedding:0.6b (639MB, 1024 dims, 32K context, MTEB 64.33) — the new leader in quality-per-byte. Outscores every sub-1GB model on multilingual benchmarks. The 32K context window is ideal for long documents. Downside: newer, less community tooling. (3) mxbai-embed-large (335M params, 1024 dims, 512 context, MTEB 64.7) — highest raw quality among popular local models, but the 512-token context is a severe limitation for markdown notes. Best for short chunks. (4) bge-m3 (567M, 1024 dims, multilingual, MTEB 64.5) — best for non-English content, supports sparse+multi-vector modes. (5) snowflake-arctic-embed2 (568M, 1024 dims, 8192 context, Apache 2.0) — only permissively licensed model in this group, good for commercial use. For the user's setup (iGPU, 8GB VRAM, markdown notes), nomic-embed-text v1.5 is the safest choice—it's tiny, battle-tested, handles long context, and leaves VRAM for the chat model. qwen3-embedding:0.6b is the upgrade path if quality matters more than ecosystem maturity. Avoid mxbai for this use case due to 512-token truncation.
no_vector_db_options: Several viable alternatives exist, each with tradeoffs: (1) sqlite-vec — A single-file SQLite extension for vector search. Excellent for embedded/local-first apps, runs anywhere (WASM, mobile, Raspberry Pi). Brute-force scans handle 100k-1M vectors in tens of milliseconds. However, ANN indexes (HNSW/IVF) are not yet production-ready, so query time degrades linearly with scale. For 50k chunks, expect ~50-100ms queries—acceptable but not ideal. Writes are fast (no full index rebuild). Best if you want zero separate infrastructure and can tolerate slightly higher latency. (2) In-memory FAISS with periodic serialization — Fastest query performance (milliseconds for 100k+ vectors), but requires manual index serialization to disk, no SQL interface, no ACID transactions, and the entire index must fit in RAM. Fragile for real-time updates (need to rebuild index on writes). Only recommended for read-heavy, batch-updated workloads. (3) Graphify's existing graph — NOT a replacement for semantic search. Graphify builds a structural knowledge graph (AST analysis + community detection) that excels at code navigation and relationship queries but cannot answer 'find notes about X concept' without embeddings. The graph captures intentional links (wiki-links) but not semantic similarity. It's complementary, not substitutive. (4) BM25/hybrid search — BM25 alone (via SQLite FTS5 or Postgres tsvector) handles exact-keyword queries well but fails on synonyms and conceptual matches. Hybrid search (BM25 + vector, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion) is the production standard in 2025-2026—it catches both exact identifiers and semantic matches. On benchmarks, hybrid lifts NDCG by 7-10% over either alone. This should be layered on top of any vector approach. (5) LLM-based retrieval — Sending chunks to an LLM for relevance scoring is accurate but prohibitively slow (100-300ms per query) and expensive at scale. Only viable for reranking top-10 results, not primary retrieval. Verdict: sqlite-vec is the best 'no vector DB' option for this use case, but pgvector + BM25 hybrid is strictly better if Postgres is available.
real_world_reliability: In 2025-2026, the most reliable personal knowledge base setups use: (1) pgvector + HNSW index + nomic-embed-text — this is the 'boring' choice that works. People report years of stable operation with zero maintenance beyond Postgres backups. The key failure mode is HNSW index bloat after heavy updates, fixed by periodic REINDEX CONCURRENTLY. (2) Qdrant self-hosted — stable but requires more ops (separate container, snapshot backups, monitoring). Some users report WAL corruption on unclean shutdowns. (3) sqlite-vec — stable for local apps, but the lack of ANN means query latency grows linearly; fine for <100k vectors. (4) ChromaDB — frequently cited in 'it just broke' reports: data loss on container restart, no proper replication, poor performance beyond 100k vectors. Not recommended for anything you care about. What breaks in practice: (a) embedding model changes—re-embedding 50k notes takes hours and must be done atomically; (b) chunking strategy—too-small chunks destroy context, too-large chunks dilute semantic signals; 500 tokens with 50-token overlap is the consensus sweet spot for markdown; (c) real-time sync—file watchers that re-index on every keystroke cause thrashing; debounce by 30-60 seconds; (d) dimension mismatch—switching embedding models requires full re-index with zero-downtime migration (create new column, backfill, swap). What's overkill: Milvus, Weaviate, and distributed vector DBs for personal use. They're designed for 100M+ vectors and multi-tenant scale—running them for 50k notes is like using Kubernetes for a static blog. The most successful personal setups in 2026 use a simple pipeline: file watcher → chunker → embedder → pgvector upsert → hybrid query (BM25 + vector via RRF). Total infrastructure: one Postgres instance, one Python script, one cron job.
recommendation: Use PostgreSQL + pgvector with HNSW index, nomic-embed-text v1.5 embeddings (via Ollama at 10.1.1.10:11434), and a hybrid BM25+vector retrieval layer. Architecture: (1) File watcher (inotify/fswatch) detects new/changed markdown files in the Obsidian vault, debounced by 30 seconds. (2) Chunker splits notes into 500-token segments with 50-token overlap, preserving header hierarchy. (3) Embedder calls Ollama's /api/embeddings endpoint with nomic-embed-text v1.5 (768-dim vectors). (4) Upsert into pgvector table (file_path, chunk_index, content, embedding, updated_at) using ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. (5) Create HNSW index with m=16, ef_construction=64; set hnsw.ef_search=100 at query time. (6) For search, run BM25 via Postgres tsvector in parallel with vector cosine distance, fuse results via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (k=60). Why this wins: (a) Zero new infrastructure—uses existing Postgres and Ollama. (b) Real-time updates are trivial—just upsert changed chunks; HNSW handles incremental writes without rebuilds. (c) Low maintenance—pgvector is a Postgres extension, not a separate service; backups are just pg_dump; monitoring is pg_stat_statements. (d) Reliable—ACID transactions mean no silent corruption; if the server crashes, the index is consistent on restart. (e) Quality—hybrid search catches both exact matches (SKU codes, function names) and semantic matches (synonyms, related concepts). (f) Scales to 10M+ vectors without architecture change. (g) If you later want to upgrade embeddings, add a new column and backfill asynchronously. Alternative considered: sqlite-vec would eliminate the separate Postgres dependency, but you lose SQL joins, ACID transactions, and the ability to run BM25 in the same query. For a setup that already has Postgres available, pgvector is strictly better. The only reason to choose sqlite-vec is if you want a single-file, embeddable database with no server process.
key_tradeoffs: pgvector vs sqlite-vec: pgvector wins on query performance (HNSW index vs linear scan), SQL integration (JOINs, transactions, BM25 in same query), and operational maturity. sqlite-vec wins on deployment simplicity (single file, no server) and portability (runs in browser/WASM). For 50k chunks, pgvector HNSW queries are ~5ms; sqlite-vec brute-force is ~50-100ms. Both are acceptable for interactive search. pgvector vs Qdrant: Qdrant has better tail latency (p99) and more sophisticated filtering, but requires a separate service, has no native hybrid search, and adds operational burden. At <1M vectors, pgvector's performance is comparable and it's simpler to maintain. Choose Qdrant only if you need complex payload filtering at scale. nomic-embed-text vs qwen3-embedding:0.6b: nomic is 23MB vs 639MB, has 4x more Ollama pulls (better ecosystem support), and handles 8192-token context. qwen3 scores ~2 points higher on MTEB and supports 32K context. For markdown notes where context length matters more than marginal MTEB gains, nomic is the pragmatic choice. Upgrade to qwen3 if you need multilingual support or maximum quality. Hybrid (BM25 + vector) vs vector-only: Hybrid adds ~5ms query latency (BM25 is fast) but improves NDCG by 7-10%. For personal knowledge bases where queries mix exact terms ('OAuth2') and concepts ('authentication flow'), hybrid is essential. Pure vector search fails on rare identifiers; pure BM25 fails on synonyms. The cost is minimal—Postgres tsvector is built-in. Real-time sync approaches: (a) File watcher + debounce (30s) — simplest, catches all changes, but re-embeds entire file on any edit. (b) Incremental diff — only re-embed changed chunks, but requires stable chunk IDs across edits. (c) Full rebuild nightly — simplest but not real-time. For 50k notes, option (a) with 30s debounce is fine—a typical edit session triggers one re-index, not dozens.
